description: The walk crosses the Boundary Road which divides Westminster and Camden and focuses on projects that represent ground-breaking trends in architecture of 1960-70s while also reflecting on the era's passing and its long-lasting influences.

events.name: Crossing the boundary, breaking the ground walkingtour

factsheet.heading: About the tour and guide
paragraphs:
Crossing the Boundary explores four groundbreaking post-war buildings on the borders of Westminster and Camden. From hospital and school to housing estate and library, discover how architects of the 1950s–70s broke with the past, reimagined civic life and created bold solutions for the future.
In the post-war decades, municipal authorities and private institutions built with exceptional confidence. Housing estates, hospitals, schools and cultural centres were intended not only to repair cities damaged by war and neglect, but to establish new models for living, learning, healing and collective life. Their architects deliberately crossed familiar boundaries, breaking with historical forms and using new materials, structures and planning ideas to define the future.
More than 50 years after these buildings were designed, the ideas they represent still resonate with some of today’s most urgent questions: the housing crisis, the scale and ambition of public investment and, more broadly, the role of architecture in shaping and organising society. Were these highly specialised designs genuinely adaptable, or were they too closely tied to their original functions? And when a building combines several uses, does that make it more resilient—or more difficult to change?
The four projects on this walk—built from the 1960s into the 1970s—offer different answers. A private hospital and school experimented with comfort, technology and new ways of organising care and education. A public housing estate and library turned architecture into a wider civic proposition about equality, shared resources and the quality of everyday life. What kinds of innovation did private control enable, and what greater social ambitions became possible through public investment?
Rather than treating these buildings either as heroic monuments or obsolete mistakes, Crossing the Boundary asks how well their original ideas still work. At each stop, we will test their multifunctionality and their capacity for flexibility, conversion and expansion. Which architectural boundaries did they cross, which ideas remain relevant, and what should be preserved, adapted or reconsidered today?
About the guide: Olga is a historian passionate about architecture and urban planning. Her role at Sir John Soane’s Museum fuels her understanding of design history, while exploring the built environment on foot allows her to examine architectural ideas directly from the pavement.

factsheet.heading: About the Golden Key Academy
paragraphs: This tour is led by one of the alumni of Open City’s Golden Key Academy – a course training up insightful and engaging guides dedicated to explaining London and bringing its many stories to life.
It is part of a wider collection of tours created by Golden Key Academy guides for the Open House Festival celebrating their conclusion of the eight month course.
Further info on the Golden Key Academy can be found here https://open-city.org.uk/golden-key-academy
